new_statements.quote: This schwa deletion seems to be occurring on a sesquisyllable, a prominent feature in Tibeto-Burman languages (Matisoff: 1973). This kind of syllable is a bi-syllabic word which has an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable. These unstressed syllables are usually a prefix followed by the main root: prefix+root- as in kə̄-réŋ ‘garden’. [p. 187] … A prosodic features such as stress, rhythm and intonation patterns will be an important feature to study in future. [p. 198]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Liangmai is a tone language (four contrastive level tones; the syllable is the tone-bearing unit). The only stress claim is that in sesquisyllabic disyllables (typically prefix + root, e.g. kə̄-réŋ 'garden') the first, prefix syllable is unstressed and the root syllable that follows is stressed, which licenses schwa deletion in fast speech. No general word-stress rule is given; the author explicitly leaves stress, rhythm and intonation for future study.
new_statements.exceptions: Schwa deletion also applies to bisyllabic root morphemes that are not prefix+root (/məwi/ → [mui] 'grow', /kə̄río/ → [krío] 'insert'); the stress characterisation is not explicitly extended to these.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, restricted to sesquisyllabic (prefix+root) disyllables; observed via fast-speech schwa deletion. Author's data mainly from the North Eastern Liangmai area but claims to cover all varieties studied.
new_statements.identity_note: Mataina 2022 describes Liangmai (lian1251) generally, drawing mainly on the North Eastern Liangmai area (author's Maguilong village) but claiming the tone facts for all varieties he has studied; he groups Liangmai villages into five dialect areas (North Eastern, Central, South Eastern, South Western, Nagaland/Ntu). No separate Glottolog dialect codes are involved. The earlier theses each describe a village variety (Widinibou 2011: Kabangning/North Eastern; Daimai G. 2016: Thalon/South Western; Raguibou 2015: Namtiram/South Western).

sources.note: Tone language with four contrastive level tones (H, M, L, extra-L); syllable is the TBU. Only stress remarks: p.187 (§4.2 schwa deletion) describes the sesquisyllable as 'a bi-syllabic word which has an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable', the unstressed syllable usually a prefix before the root (kə̄-réŋ 'garden'); p.198 (conclusion) says stress, rhythm and intonation remain to be studied. No general stress-placement rule.
